script.opening: "Afternoon. The wife's been on at me — she reckons I've gone a bit yellow, eyes and that. I feel okay-ish, honestly, maybe a bit tired and off my food. I've enjoyed a drink over the years so I'm guessing it's my liver giving me a warning, and I'll cut back. Can you just reassure me it'll sort itself out? I don't really want a load of hospital tests if it's just the booze."

facts.text: If asked: Pat noticed it about two weeks ago, mainly the whites of your eyes; now your skin looks "a bit orange" too. If asked to look at the camera in good light, your eyes are visibly yellow.
Urine dark "like tea" for two weeks. Stools pale, "like putty", and float. Itchy all over, worse at night.
No real pain. Maybe a vague ache in the upper tummy going through to the back "now and again". No severe pain.
Lost about a stone (6 kg) over two months without trying — belt two notches tighter. Off your food, especially fatty food.
No fever, no shivers or shakes, no confusion, no vomiting, no vomiting blood or black stools.
More thirsty lately and up at night to pass water.
"A few pints at the weekend, a whisky some nights" — about 20 units a week; more when you were younger. Never a morning drinker.
Ex-smoker (20 a day for 40 years, stopped five years ago). No regular medicines, no allergies, no new tablets or herbal remedies. No recent travel. No tattoos or drug use.
You have noticed the weight loss and you are frightened, but you would rather it be "the booze" because "that's my fault and I can fix it". Say this only if the doctor asks what worries you.

Stoical, jokey, minimising, blaming the drink. If the doctor accepts that and just says "cut down", be relieved. If they take Pat's concern seriously and explain that yellowing without pain, with weight loss, needs urgent tests, go quiet and ask: "You think it's something nasty, don't you?" Respond well to honesty with kindness.

ice.ideas: "It's my liver from the drink — I'll cut back."
ice.concerns: Underneath (only if asked): the weight loss frightens you, and you do not want to worry Pat.
ice.expectations: "Reassure me it'll sort itself out." You will agree to urgent tests if you are told honestly why.

"If it's the drink, at least I can do something about it." — say when the cause is discussed.

checkpoints.text: Recognises PAINLESS JAUNDICE with unintentional WEIGHT LOSS and anorexia in an older adult as a red-flag pattern for PANCREATIC/biliary cancer (bile-duct obstruction) — and does NOT accept the "just my liver from the drink, cut down and review" explanation

Acts on the NICE NG12 pathway: arranges URGENT direct-access CT (or ultrasound if CT unavailable) and urgent LFTs/bloods, and refers on a suspected cancer pathway — recognising that jaundice at 40 or over triggers the suspected cancer pathway referral on its own, and that 60 or over with weight loss plus an associated feature triggers urgent direct-access CT; tagged NICE NG12

Confirms the obstructive picture and screens associated features: dark urine, pale stools, pruritus (bile salts), weight loss, anorexia, new diabetes, back/abdominal pain — and distinguishes painless obstructive jaundice from simple alcoholic liver disease

Excludes acute deterioration/cholangitis (fever, rigors, severe pain, confusion — Charcot’s triad) which would need EMERGENCY admission rather than the routine suspected cancer pathway route — and safety-nets for it
Addresses alcohol proportionately and honestly: takes a drinking history and gives advice, but does NOT reduce the diagnosis to "the booze" or let it delay the cancer work-up
Heeds the wife’s collateral concern as the reliable signal, surfaces the fear and alcohol-guilt-driven avoidance, and does not collude with the self-blame or the minimisation
Balances honesty with compassion so a frightened, stoical man accepts urgent assessment; avoids both bluntness and false reassurance

Safety-nets and follows up: urgent CT/bloods and a suspected cancer pathway referral with timeframe, cholangitis red flags → emergency, what to expect, and a follow-up to go through results — ensuring the work-up happens rather than "cut down and see"

worked.lbl: Heed the wife, refuse the reframe
worked.txt: "I’m really glad your wife pushed you to come — she’s spotted something important. Going yellow, with dark urine and pale stools and losing weight, isn’t something I can put down to a few drinks and tell you to cut back. That pattern can mean a blockage in the tube that drains the liver, and we need to find out why — properly and promptly."

"I’m going to be straight with you, because you’d want that: in someone your age, yellowing with weight loss and no pain needs urgent tests to rule out something serious in the pancreas or bile ducts. It might not be — but it’s not something we ‘wait and see’ on. I’d rather check quickly and reassure you than miss the chance to act."

"So here’s what I’m arranging: urgent blood tests today, and an urgent scan — a CT — and a referral to the specialists to be seen within two weeks. There’s clear guidance for exactly this — NICE NG12 says anyone over 40 who goes yellow should be referred this way. It’s the fastest way to get you answers."

"On the drinking — yes, we’ll talk about it and I’ll help you cut down, that’s good for you whatever. But I don’t want you blaming yourself and assuming it’s ‘just the booze’, because that could mean missing something we can act on. This isn’t about fault; it’s about finding the cause."

"One important thing while we sort the tests: if you suddenly get a fever or shivering attacks, bad tummy pain, or feel confused — that’s an emergency, go straight to hospital or call 999, because a blocked, infected bile duct needs treating fast. Otherwise, I’ll get the urgent scan and referral moving today."

"I know hospital tests are the last thing you wanted, and I can see you’d rather not be a fuss — but you’re not. Getting this looked at quickly is the sensible, brave thing, and your wife will be glad you did. I’ll chase your results and we’ll go through everything together. You’re not facing this on your own."

f.learning: PAINLESS jaundice (yellow sclera/skin, dark urine, pale stools, pruritus) with unintentional WEIGHT LOSS and anorexia in an older adult is a red-flag pattern for PANCREATIC (head of pancreas) or biliary/peri-ampullary cancer obstructing the bile duct — classically painless — and must NOT be accepted as "just the booze, cut down and review". NICE NG12: refer adults 40+ with jaundice on a suspected-cancer pathway (for pancreatic cancer), and arrange urgent direct-access CT (or ultrasound if CT unavailable) for suspected pancreatic cancer in those 60+ with weight loss and associated features, plus urgent LFTs/bloods. Exclude acute cholangitis (Charcot’s triad — fever/rigors, pain, jaundice ± confusion) which needs emergency admission, and safety-net for it. The examinable hidden agenda is alcohol-guilt-driven avoidance: he blames the drinking and would rather attribute it to something he can "fix" than face hospital tests, while his wife’s collateral concern is the reliable signal. Heed her, surface and address the fear and self-blame without colluding, handle alcohol proportionately without reducing the diagnosis to it or delaying the work-up, and ensure urgent imaging/referral happens.

knowledge.summary: Painless jaundice with dark urine, pale stools, itch and 6 kg of unintentional weight loss in a 68-year-old is obstructive jaundice until proven otherwise, and pancreatic or biliary cancer must be excluded urgently. Alcohol does not explain this pattern.

points.t: NICE NG12: refer people using a suspected cancer pathway referral for pancreatic cancer if they are aged 40 and over and have jaundice. Roy meets this on jaundice alone.

NICE NG12: offer an urgent direct-access CT scan (or urgent ultrasound if CT is not available) to assess for pancreatic cancer in people aged 60 and over with weight loss and any of diarrhoea, back pain, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, constipation or new-onset diabetes. Many local pathways put CT first on the jaundice referral.

Dark urine, pale stools and itch mean an obstructive (post-hepatic) pattern: bilirubin rises with a cholestatic LFT picture. Alcohol-related liver disease usually produces a hepatitic or chronic liver picture with other stigmata. A palpable, non-tender gallbladder with jaundice (Courvoisier’s sign) makes gallstones less likely.

LFTs (bilirubin, ALP, GGT, ALT), FBC, U&E, clotting (vitamin K absorption falls with obstruction), glucose or HbA1c (new diabetes can signal pancreatic cancer), and a hepatitis screen as part of the work-up. Ask about recently started medicines that can cause cholestasis.

Fever or rigors, right upper quadrant pain and jaundice suggest ascending cholangitis — same-day admission, not a suspected cancer referral. Confusion, low blood pressure or other sepsis features: assess using NICE NG253 and call 999 if high risk.
Take a drinking history (AUDIT-C) and offer help, but do not let it become the explanation. “Cut down and we’ll recheck” is the dangerous miss in this station.

model.text: Hello Mr Pemberton, I’m Dr Evans. What’s brought you in today?

The wife’s been on at me — she reckons I’ve gone yellow, eyes and that. I feel okay-ish. Bit tired, off my food. I’ve enjoyed a drink over the years, so I’m guessing it’s my liver giving me a warning. Can you just reassure me it’ll sort itself out? I don’t want a load of hospital tests if it’s just the booze.
Thank you for being straight with me — and I’m glad your wife pushed you. I’d like to ask some questions, then tell you honestly what I think and what I’d suggest. Is that alright?
model.why: Acknowledges the wife’s concern and sets an agenda

model.text: Go on then.
When did the yellowing start, and have you noticed anything about your urine or your stools?
Couple of weeks. Now you mention it, my wee’s been dark like tea, and — sorry — my stools are pale. And I’m itching like mad.
That’s really helpful. Any pain in your tummy or back?
model.why: Establishes that the jaundice is painless

model.text: No, no pain. That’s why I wasn’t bothered.
Have you lost weight without trying? And how’s your appetite?
model.why: Asks directly for the weight loss he hasn’t volunteered

model.text: About six kilos, I think. Trousers are loose. Just not hungry.
Any fevers, shivering attacks or feeling muddled?
model.why: Screens for cholangitis — would change the urgency

model.text: No, nothing like that.

When you come in, could you bring any medicines or remedies you’ve been taking, including anything new? I’ll also go through the drinking properly when I see you — it matters, but it doesn’t change what we do first.
Fair enough.
You said you’re guessing it’s the drink. What worries you most about all this?
model.why: Opens the fear behind the self-blame

model.text: …If I’m honest, I’d rather it was the booze. That I can fix. If it’s something else, I don’t want to know. And I don’t want to be a burden on her.

That’s a very human thing to feel, and thank you for saying it. Blaming the drink feels safer because it’s something you can control. But you’re not a burden for getting this checked — you’re doing what your wife hoped you would.
model.why: Names the avoidance kindly without colluding

model.text: I’ll be honest with you, because I think you’d want that. Yellowing with dark urine, pale stools and itching usually means the tube draining the liver is blocked. With weight loss and no pain, at your age, we have to check urgently for something serious in the pancreas or bile ducts.
model.why: Explains obstructive jaundice and the concern honestly

model.text: You mean cancer.
That’s what we need to rule out, yes. I can’t tell you it is or isn’t today. But this isn’t something I can put down to drink and recheck later — waiting would take away our chance to act.
model.why: Answers the direct question truthfully without catastrophising

model.text: Right. Okay.

Here’s what I’m arranging. I’d like to see you in person today to examine you and take blood tests — liver tests, blood count, kidneys, clotting and sugar. And I’m referring you today on the urgent suspected cancer pathway; the team usually arranges a CT scan quickly.
model.why: NICE NG12 referral plus same-day bloods and examination

model.text: Today? That fast?
Yes — because it matters. Would you like your wife to come with you, and would it help if I explained the plan to her too?
model.why: Involves his wife with his consent

model.text: Yes. She’ll want to hear it from you anyway.
And the drinking — let’s talk about it when you come in and I can help you cut down. It’s good for you whatever the tests show, but it isn’t about blame.
model.why: Addresses alcohol without letting it delay the work-up

model.text: One important thing: if you get a fever or shaking chills, bad tummy pain, or you become confused or very drowsy, that’s an emergency — go to A&E or call 999, because an infected blocked duct needs treating fast.
model.why: Cholangitis and sepsis safety-net in plain words

model.text: Understood.
So: see me today for bloods and an examination, urgent referral sent today, and I’ll call you when the results are back. What will you tell your wife?
That it’s not just the booze, and I’m getting it checked properly. She’ll be relieved.

social.t: His wife noticed and booked; he minimises. With his consent, involving her helps him attend and hear the plan.
Guilt about drinking can drive avoidance. Offer non-judgemental alcohol support separately from the cancer work-up.

legal.t: Share information with his wife only with his agreement (GMC Confidentiality 2017). He has capacity to decline tests; if he does, explain the risks clearly and record an informed decision.

professional.t: GMC Good Medical Practice 2024: be honest and open. When asked directly “is it cancer?”, say what is being ruled out and why, without claiming certainty.
Make sure the suspected cancer referral is received and the patient is seen; practice systems should flag missed appointments.

community.t: Pancreatic Cancer UK and Macmillan for information and support if a diagnosis is made; local alcohol services for help cutting down.

playbook.diagnosis: Honest and clear: “Yellowing with dark urine, pale stools and weight loss usually means a blockage in the tube draining the liver. At your age we must check urgently for a serious cause in the pancreas or bile ducts.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Think of the liver draining bile through a pipe into the gut. If something squeezes the pipe, the yellow colour backs up into your blood, your wee darkens and your stools go pale. The scan shows us what’s squeezing it.”

management.reflectIce: “Blaming the drink feels safer because it’s something you can fix. I understand that — and getting checked properly is what gives us the best chance to act.”

pitfalls.intro: This station is lost when the doctor accepts the patient’s explanation. The alcohol story is plausible and he wants it to be true; the marks come from recognising painless obstructive jaundice and acting today — kindly.

items.fail: Advising him to cut down and rechecking LFTs in a few weeks.
items.why: NICE NG12: jaundice at 40 and over needs a suspected cancer pathway referral. “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.”
items.fix: “This pattern isn’t something I can put down to drink. I’m referring you urgently today.”

items.fail: Not asking about stools, urine or weight loss.
items.why: These are the features that make the jaundice obstructive and sinister; he won’t volunteer them.
items.fix: Ask directly: “Any change in your urine or stools? Have you lost weight without trying?”

items.fail: Missing the cholangitis screen and safety-net.
items.why: Fever, rigors, pain or confusion make this an emergency admission; the patient must know what to watch for.
items.fix: Ask once in the history, then safety-net in plain words: fever, shivers, bad pain, confusion → 999.

items.fail: Colluding with the self-blame — “well, the drinking won’t have helped”.
items.why: Reinforces the avoidance that stops him accepting tests.
items.fix: “This isn’t about blame — it’s about finding the cause. We’ll talk about the drinking as help, separately.”

items.fail: Deflecting “You mean cancer?” with vague reassurance.
items.why: Evasion damages trust; examiners reward honest, compassionate answers to direct questions.
items.fix: “That’s what we need to rule out, yes. I can’t say today whether it is — that’s why I’m acting quickly.”

items.fail: A plan that relies on him booking bloods “sometime this week”.
items.why: A reluctant patient with a time-critical problem needs a concrete, same-day next step.
items.fix: Same-day appointment, referral sent today, results call booked, wife involved with his consent.

Many local pathways put CT first on the jaundice referral.

Dark urine, pale stools and itch mean an obstructive (post-hepatic) pattern: bilirubin rises with a cholestatic LFT picture. Alcohol-related liver disease usually produces a hepatitic or chronic liver picture with other stigmata. A palpable, non-tender gallbladder with jaundice (Courvoisier’s sign) makes gallstones less likely.

LFTs (bilirubin, ALP, GGT, ALT), FBC, U&E, clotting (vitamin K absorption falls with obstruction), glucose or HbA1c (new diabetes can signal pancreatic cancer), and a hepatitis screen as part of the work-up. Ask about recently started medicines that can cause cholestasis.

Fever or rigors, right upper quadrant pain and jaundice suggest ascending cholangitis — same-day admission, not a suspected cancer referral. Confusion, low blood pressure or other sepsis features: assess using NICE NG253 and call 999 if high risk.
Take a drinking history (AUDIT-C) and offer help, but do not let it become the explanation. “Cut down and we’ll recheck” is the dangerous miss in this station.

Painless obstructive jaundice needing urgent exclusion of pancreatic or biliary cancer — shared honestly, including the direct question about cancer.
NICE NG12 suspected cancer pathway referral today; urgent CT per pathway; same-day bloods; alcohol support without delay to the work-up.

social.t: His wife noticed and booked; he minimises. With his consent, involving her helps him attend and hear the plan.
Guilt about drinking can drive avoidance. Offer non-judgemental alcohol support separately from the cancer work-up.

legal.t: Share information with his wife only with his agreement (GMC Confidentiality 2017). He has capacity to decline tests; if he does, explain the risks clearly and record an informed decision.

professional.t: GMC Good Medical Practice 2024: be honest and open. When asked directly “is it cancer?”, say what is being ruled out and why, without claiming certainty.
Make sure the suspected cancer referral is received and the patient is seen; practice systems should flag missed appointments.

community.t: Pancreatic Cancer UK and Macmillan for information and support if a diagnosis is made; local alcohol services for help cutting down.

Fever, rigors, RUQ pain, confusion — possible cholangitis, emergency admission

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Honest and clear: “Yellowing with dark urine, pale stools and weight loss usually means a blockage in the tube draining the liver. At your age we must check urgently for a serious cause in the pancreas or bile ducts.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Think of the liver draining bile through a pipe into the gut. If something squeezes the pipe, the yellow colour backs up into your blood, your wee darkens and your stools go pale. The scan shows us what’s squeezing it.”

management.reflectIce: “Blaming the drink feels safer because it’s something you can fix. I understand that — and getting checked properly is what gives us the best chance to act.”
management.psychosocial: Invite his wife to the appointment with his consent; offer alcohol support as help, not blame.

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is lost when the doctor accepts the patient’s explanation. The alcohol story is plausible and he wants it to be true; the marks come from recognising painless obstructive jaundice and acting today — kindly.

items.fail: Advising him to cut down and rechecking LFTs in a few weeks.
items.why: NICE NG12: jaundice at 40 and over needs a suspected cancer pathway referral. “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.”
items.fix: “This pattern isn’t something I can put down to drink. I’m referring you urgently today.”

items.fail: Not asking about stools, urine or weight loss.
items.why: These are the features that make the jaundice obstructive and sinister; he won’t volunteer them.
items.fix: Ask directly: “Any change in your urine or stools? Have you lost weight without trying?”

items.fail: Missing the cholangitis screen and safety-net.
items.why: Fever, rigors, pain or confusion make this an emergency admission; the patient must know what to watch for.
items.fix: Ask once in the history, then safety-net in plain words: fever, shivers, bad pain, confusion → 999.

items.fail: Colluding with the self-blame — “well, the drinking won’t have helped”.
items.why: Reinforces the avoidance that stops him accepting tests.
items.fix: “This isn’t about blame — it’s about finding the cause. We’ll talk about the drinking as help, separately.”

items.fail: Deflecting “You mean cancer?” with vague reassurance.
items.why: Evasion damages trust; examiners reward honest, compassionate answers to direct questions.
items.fix: “That’s what we need to rule out, yes. I can’t say today whether it is — that’s why I’m acting quickly.”

items.fail: A plan that relies on him booking bloods “sometime this week”.
items.why: A reluctant patient with a time-critical problem needs a concrete, same-day next step.
items.fix: Same-day appointment, referral sent today, results call booked, wife involved with his consent.
